title: Chapter 17. Of the Causes, Generation, and Definition of a Common-wealth
paragraphs: Men naturally love liberty, and they love holding power over others. Why, then, do they accept the restraint we see them living under in commonwealths? The final cause, end, or design behind it is this: they foresee their own preservation, and a more contented life along with it. That is to say, they see a way out of that miserable condition of war which, as has already been shown, follows necessarily from men's natural passions whenever there is no visible power to keep them in awe and to bind them, through fear of punishment, to perform their covenants and to observe those laws of nature set down in the fourteenth and fifteenth chapters.

For the laws of nature—justice, equity, modesty, mercy, and, in sum, doing to others as we would be done to—are in themselves, without the terror of some power to make them be observed, contrary to our natural passions, which carry us toward partiality, pride, revenge, and the like. And covenants without the sword are only words, with no strength to secure a man at all. So despite the laws of nature (which each man has kept only when he has the will to keep them and can do so safely), if no power is set up, or none great enough for our security, every man will rely, and may lawfully rely, on his own strength and skill as a safeguard against all other men. In every place where men have lived in small families, robbing and plundering one another has been a trade, and so far from being thought contrary to the law of nature that the greater the plunder they took, the greater their honor. In that business men observed no laws but the laws of honor: that is, to abstain from cruelty, leaving men their lives and their farming tools. And what small families did then, cities and kingdoms do now, for they are only larger families. For their own security they enlarge their dominions on any pretext of danger or fear of invasion, or of aid that might be given to invaders; and they do all they can to subdue or weaken their neighbors, by open force and by covert arts, for want of any other safeguard—and they do it justly, and are remembered for it with honor in later ages.

Nor is it the joining together of a small number of men that gives them this security. Where the numbers are small, a slight addition on one side or the other makes the advantage in strength great enough to decide the victory, and so gives encouragement to an invasion. The multitude we can trust for our security is not fixed at any particular number; it is set by comparison with the enemy we fear. It is sufficient when the enemy's advantage is not so plain and conspicuous as to settle the outcome of a war, and therefore not enough to move him to make the attempt.

And let the multitude be as great as you like: if their actions are directed by their own individual judgments and individual appetites, they can expect no defense or protection from it, neither against a common enemy nor against the injuries they do one another. Being divided in opinion about the best use and application of their strength, they do not help but hinder one another, and by working against each other they reduce their strength to nothing. As a result they are easily subdued by a very few who act in agreement; and even when there is no common enemy, they make war on one another over their private interests. For if we could suppose a great multitude of men agreeing to observe justice and the other laws of nature without a common power to keep them all in awe, we might just as well suppose all mankind doing the same—and then there would be no civil government or commonwealth at all, nor any need of one, because there would be peace without subjection.

Nor is it enough, for the security men want to last their whole lives, that they be governed and directed by a single judgment for a limited time, as in one battle or one war. For though their united effort may win them a victory against a foreign enemy, afterward—when they either have no common enemy, or when the man one party counts an enemy another party counts a friend—the difference in their interests must break them apart and drop them back into war among themselves.

It is true that certain living creatures, such as bees and ants, live sociably with one another (which is why Aristotle counted them among the political creatures), and yet they have no direction beyond their individual judgments and appetites, and no speech by which one of them can tell another what he thinks would serve the common benefit. So someone may perhaps want to know why mankind cannot do the same. To which I answer:

First, that men are continually in competition for honor and dignity, which these creatures are not. Among men this competition breeds envy and hatred, and in the end war; among these creatures it does not.

Secondly, that among these creatures the common good does not differ from the private good; and since they are inclined by nature toward their private good, they produce the common benefit by doing so. But man, whose joy consists in comparing himself with other men, can relish nothing but what sets him above them.

Thirdly, that these creatures, not having the use of reason as man does, neither see nor think they see any fault in how their common business is managed. Among men, by contrast, there are a great many who think themselves wiser and abler to govern the public than the rest; and these men strive to reform and innovate, one in this direction, another in that, and so bring it into disorder and civil war.

Fourthly, that these creatures, though they have some use of voice for making their desires and other feelings known to one another, lack that art of words by which some men can present to others what is good in the likeness of evil, and what is evil in the likeness of good, and can magnify or shrink the apparent size of good and evil, making men discontented and troubling their peace whenever they please.

Fifthly, that creatures without reason cannot tell the difference between injury and damage; and therefore, as long as they are comfortable, they take no offense at their fellows. Man, on the other hand, is most troublesome when he is most at ease, for that is when he loves to display his wisdom and to check the actions of those who govern the commonwealth.

Lastly, that the agreement of these creatures is natural, whereas that of men is only by covenant, which is artificial. It is no wonder, then, if something more than covenant is required to make their agreement constant and lasting—namely a common power to keep them in awe and to direct their actions toward the common benefit.

There is only one way to set up such a common power, able to defend them from invasion by foreigners and from the injuries they do one another, and so to secure them well enough that by their own industry and the fruits of the earth they may feed themselves and live contentedly. It is to confer all their power and strength on one man, or on one assembly of men, who can reduce all their wills, by majority of voices, to one will. That is as much as to say: to appoint one man, or one assembly of men, to bear their Person; and for every one of them to own and acknowledge himself to be the Author of whatever the bearer of their Person shall do, or cause to be done, in matters concerning the common peace and safety; and in this to submit their wills, every one, to his will, and their judgments to his judgment. This is more than consent or concord. It is a real unity of them all in one and the same Person, made by a covenant of every man with every man, as if every man should say to every man, "I Authorise and give up my Right of Governing my selfe, to this Man, or to this Assembly of men, on this condition, that thou give up thy Right to him, and Authorise all his Actions in like manner." Once this is done, the multitude so united in one Person is called a COMMONWEALTH, in Latin CIVITAS. This is the generation of that great LEVIATHAN, or rather—to speak more reverently—of that Mortal God, to whom, under the Immortal God, we owe our peace and defense. For by this authority, given him by every particular man in the commonwealth, he has the use of so much power and strength conferred on him that, by the terror of it, he is able to shape the wills of them all toward peace at home and mutual aid against their enemies abroad.

And in him consists the essence of the commonwealth, which—to define it—is "One Person, of whose Acts a great Multitude, by mutuall Covenants one with another, have made themselves every one the Author, to the end he may use the strength and means of them all, as he shall think expedient, for their Peace and Common Defence."
And the one who carries this Person is called the SOVEREIGN, and is said to have sovereign power; and everyone else is his SUBJECT.

This sovereign power is attained in two ways. One is by natural force: as when a man makes his children submit themselves and their children to his government, since he is able to destroy them if they refuse; or when by war he subdues his enemies to his will and grants them their lives on that condition. The other is when men agree among themselves to submit voluntarily to some man, or some assembly of men, trusting to be protected by him against all others. This latter kind may be called a political commonwealth, or a commonwealth by institution; the former, a commonwealth by acquisition. And I shall speak first of a commonwealth by institution.
